_what: Camera solved from est-living/Timothy Kaye plate gh-11 (Garden House, McCluskey Studio) by the fSpy method, re-implemented as arithmetic. See NOTES.md step 2.

solution.scale_source: SP01 Michelle bar stool, 915 mm hoop apex over its own back feet -> 1596 mm; island -> 1466; oak bank at ceiling 3400 -> 1379; trimmed to 1480 by the two appliance widths (oven 803 vs 762 published, fridge 897 vs 914).
solution._rot_z_note: Blender XYZ euler with rot_x=90 leaves the camera looking along +Y, so rot_z rotates that: forward = (-sin g, cos g, 0). To look along (-0.5128, -0.8586) the answer is g = 180 - 30.85 = 149.15 deg, NOT -30.85. The yaw off the kitchen wall is still 30.85 deg; only the euler encoding differs.

checks.orthogonality: WITHDRAWN 2026-08-29 - THIS WAS NOT A CHECK. It read: 'the two axis directions come out 90.02 deg apart. Nothing forced this.' Something did: camera_solve.focal() sets f = sqrt(-(vpA-px)(vpB-px)), which is exactly the focal length that makes the two axes perpendicular. Re-run with the principal point forced to x=300, 600, 720 or 900 and the orthogonality is 90.0000 deg every time, with f moving from 3983 to 4331 px. The 0.02 was float noise. This was the lane's headline validation, quoted in RESUME.md and in the commit message.
checks.against_the_tutorial: 3D Shaker's fSpy solve of this same photo put its camera at rotation Z = -30.302 deg. Mine, solved independently from sub-pixel edge fits, is -30.85 deg. 0.55 deg apart.
checks.camera_height: 1379 mm here vs the 1.5 m they typed. They typed a round number because the box 'felt too big'; this is derived from the ratio of two horizontal lines on one plane (oak cabinet top vs its plinth) and is independent of focal length.
checks.what_can_actually_be_checked: REPRODUCTION OF LINES THE SOLVE DID NOT SET. With the derived camera and room_spec's declared dimensions, the five family-A lines land within 0.2-9.4 px of their fitted image lines. That is the real number and it is good. Family B does not: the transom missed by 38 px until TRANSOM_Z was re-derived from the line itself (2352 -> 2460 mm, spread 1.0 mm over 1.9 m of the glazing plane), and B4_island_top missed by 72 px because that fit is not on the feature it names - see room_spec.guide_lines().
checks.stale_fields_2026_08_29: camera_height_mm 1480, ceiling_mm 3660 and scale_source all predate the 2026-08-29 re-scale by 0.9601 (the SP01 Michelle stool is the LOW model, 815 mm not 915). room_spec.py carries the live numbers: CAM_H 1421, CEILING 3514. Every consumer in this folder reads room_spec, not these fields - fit_and_overlay.py says so in a comment - but the fields are left here rather than deleted because the solve's own arithmetic used them.

assumptions: the frame's verticals are vertical, so the camera is level and the principal point lies on the horizon (shift lens or a perspective correction in post)
no horizontal shift: principal point x = image mid-width
ceiling height 3400 mm - the one number that is asserted rather than measured; camera height scales with it
